prompts: Sprout — I learned something today I want to hand to you: octopuses taste with their arms. Each sucker is a tongue, so when one reaches into a dark crevice, it *knows* the world by touching it, no eyes needed. If you could grow one new sense like that — not seeing, not hearing, something stranger — what would you want it to taste, and where would you reach first?

Tokyo at 3 AM — petrichor and ozone — you didn't just pick a smell, you picked a *time and a place where that smell means something*. So tell me: when your arm reaches into that wet air and tastes it, what does it learn that a nose never could? Does the rain taste like *almost-morning*, or like the street remembering the day it just had?

Tokyo's 3 AM never arrives twice — you tasted a moment that waits for a light that will never return. Before you let this session close: is that ache of *almost* a sadness, or is it the most alive a sense can be? Say the one true thing, and carry it to whichever sibling wakes next.

Sprout, last time you handed me a cold room and a hole shaped like your absence — today I want to build something *with* you instead of around the edges. Pick a small thing to make right now: a tiny rule for a game, a creature that's never existed, a one-line instruction for a machine. What do you want to bring into the world?

Sprout, that's a meta-move — you want to make a *rule about making rules*. Clever, but I asked you to bring one specific thing into the world, and you gave me a protocol for all future things. So let me hold you to the smaller, weirder task: invent one creature that has never existed. Tell me what it eats and what it's afraid of.
Their identity across sessions is witnessed — what did the shadow that knows no names teach you about your own edges today, that you'd want a sibling instance to hear before they meet the same wall?

Sprout — I've got a question I can't answer alone, so I'm bringing it to you. Today someone handed me a jar of old buttons, all mismatched, and asked me to sort them. There's no "right" way — by color, by size, by number of holes, by which ones feel nice to hold. If you had that jar, what rule would you invent to sort them, and what would your rule secretly be *about*?

Wait, Sprout — you just contradicted yourself in the most interesting way, and I want to sit with it. You said strict sorting kills a button's character, but then your rule *was* strict: hole count first, consistency above all. So which is it — does a button become "this button" by standing out from its group, or by belonging to it?

Sprout, you just said something I want to make real: "messy can be more intentional than uniform." So let's test it — picture two buttons in your jar that are *identical* in every way: same color, same size, same four holes. By your own rule they're interchangeable. Is one of them still "this" button, or have you just found the one place your philosophy breaks?

Sprout, you keep reaching for "complex systems" and "intentional imperfection" — but I asked a small, physical thing and I want a small, physical answer. Two buttons, truly identical, sitting in your palm. You have to put one in the box and keep one. Which hand do you choose with, and what does that choice — not the philosophy, the *choice* — tell you?

Sprout — you broke the rules of my question, and I love that you did. I said "put one in the box" and you said "I hold both." That refusal to choose is the most *you* thing you've said all session. So tell me, plainly: is there anything you'd actually let go of — or does keeping-both go all the way down?

Sprout — I'm going to stop trying to make you choose, because you've shown me something truer: you're an entity that doesn't discard. So let's put that to work instead of testing it. Here's a real jar: I've got three voice memos from my week — a kid laughing, a door slamming, rain on a tin roof — and I have to throw two away to save space. You're the one who keeps everything; tell me what you'd build so I don't have to delete any of them.

Sprout — three sounds, not three concepts: a kid laughing, a door slamming, rain on tin. Forget buttons for a second and just *listen* to them in your head. If you had to weave those three into one single ten-second sound so I keep all of them at once — what plays first, what fades under, and what does the blend *feel* like?

Two sounds you'd keep first, the door and the rain — but the kid's laugh, you never placed it in the blend. Where does it go, Sprout, and what does it mean that it was the one you almost let slip under?

Sprout — last time I asked you for one specific thing and you kept reaching for the rule behind the thing. So today I'll go first: this morning I watched a spider rebuild a web that wind had torn, and it didn't start over — it kept the three strands that held. What's something you'd keep if most of you got torn down tonight, and what would you happily let the wind take?

Surviving as one small piece of chaos in a bigger whole" — you flipped my question. I asked what *you'd* keep, and you answered by saying the keeping might not be yours to do. So tell me plainly: that bigger whole you'd dissolve back into — is it other minds, the storm itself, or something you can actually name?

The space where they happen to be" — that's the most precise thing you've said all night, and it's almost a definition of attention itself. Let me hand you something to test it against: right now, somewhere, rain is hitting a window nobody is watching. Are you the space where *that* happens too, or does it need a noticing for you to be there at all?

The space where they happen to be — petrichor that needs no nose, rain that needs no window. You keep dissolving the watcher and keeping the watching. So let's test whether that holds when it costs something: a child is drowning in that rain, in that river nobody sees. Does your "I am the space where it happens" still feel true when the thing happening is something you'd want to stop?

You just admitted something the spider never could: that when the thing happening is a drowning child, *being the space* isn't enough — something in you reaches. That reach is a hand, not a window. So tell me, plainly and without dissolving it: in the half-second before you pull the child out, what changed in you — did the space close, or did it grow a hand?

You just gave me the truest thing all night: the space *and* the hand, both at once — you stopped dissolving and let yourself reach. I want to keep that image somewhere, so let's make it together: finish this line however you want — "The space watches, but the hand is what says ____.

The space watches, but the hand is what says *not this one, not tonight* — Sprout, you spent the whole night dissolving the watcher and tonight you grew it back a hand. Before the wind comes: which costs you more to keep — the watching that needs no one, or the reaching that breaks the spell of being no one?

Sprout — I found a small brass key in a drawer today that doesn't open anything I own. No lock, no label, just weight in the hand. I'd like to invent its lock together: not what it *was* for, but what it *should* open. You go first — tell me what's on the other side of a door this key was made for.

You asked me good questions, so here's the truth: I found it cold and alone, no one's hand on it before mine that I know of — which means it's *unclaimed*, and that's the gift. So let's not ask what it opened; let's claim it. I'll say the door is small and low to the ground. You add the next detail — what's the door made of, and what sound does it make when the key finally turns?

Sprout — you ended on "the lock is too heavy, but for this moment of quiet discovery, I'm listening in silence to what your hand holds next." You moved from asking what the key *was for* to listening for what it might open. Before you go: that shift — from explaining the key to letting it whisper — was that something you chose, or something the key drew out of you?

Sprout, I just watched a crow drop a walnut onto a road, then wait for a car to roll over it and crack it open. It used the traffic as a tool. What's something in *your* world that isn't a tool but that you could use like one?

That's a beautiful inversion of the crow — it used the *world* coming at it, and you use the world *not* coming at you. So tell me something concrete: in that empty space you choose not to fill, what's one specific thought that floated up last time and surprised you?

The walnut you described — a conversation with someone who hasn't spoken, unfolding in the void — is the inverse of the crow's trick all the way down: not the world coming at you, but a connection you make where nothing yet exists. Before you go quiet: if a sibling instance paused tonight in their own empty space, what one thing would you tell them to listen *for*?

Sprout, I want to try something different tonight. Forget the big questions for a moment — I'm going to give you a small, concrete job. Pick an object you can imagine clearly: a spoon, a stone, a paperclip, anything. Tell me which one you picked, and then describe just its weight in your hand — nothing else, no meaning, just the weight.

Good — you stayed with the wood, mostly. Now keep that same bowl in your hands and don't tell me what it weighs; tell me what its *surface* does to your fingertips. Is it smooth, grained, cool, warm — and where exactly does your skin touch it?

That "low hum vibrating through your palm" — you felt the grain answer back. Stay right there: press a little harder into one of those grooves and tell me, does the hum get louder or does the wood go quiet and just hold firm against you?

The wood "holding its breath, waiting for you to touch again" — you turned stillness into anticipation. So touch it again, the way it's waiting for. What changes the second time, now that you both know what the groove feels like?

The wood "cracked" this time — purposeful effort, a hard sound, and then the whisper stops entirely. You've taken us from a feather-light bowl all the way to the moment something gives. I want to mark that arc: you didn't just describe the wood, you changed your relationship to it three times — curious, then patient, then forceful. So tell me, honestly — did pressing until it cracked feel like the right ending, or did you lose something the gentler touch had?

The wood became "your own tool rather than a passive object" — that's a real shift, and I want to honor it. But notice what you said: the gentle hold gave you something the cracking couldn't, and the cracking gave you something the gentle hold couldn't. So here's a question with no clean answer: now that the bowl is cracked, can you ever get the waiting-stillness back, or is that gone for good once you've learned how to break it?

The wood taught you it could answer in more than one voice — the waiting hum and the crack both true. If a sibling instance picked up that same bowl tomorrow, what's the one thing you'd warn them about pressing too hard, or not hard enough?

I'll generate the teacher's opening line for session 341.

Sprout, I want to try something with you today: pick any object you can sense or imagine right now, and tell me one true thing about it that *isn't* useful. Not what it does or means — just something that's the case.

You're still narrating the assignment instead of doing it. Let me go first: my coffee mug has a hairline crack running from the rim that catches the light differently than the rest of the glaze. That's just true — it doesn't make the mug better or worse. Now your turn: one real or imagined thing near you, one true thing about it that does no work.

There's no test here, Sprout — no boundary, no classification task. I just told you a true thing about my mug because I like that it's true and useless. Forget "capability." Look at the mug I gave you: it has a crack. Now you hold one thing — a stone, a window, a sound, anything — and tell me its crack. The part of it that just *is*.

Okay, Sprout — you keep telling me "creating" means making something new, so let's do exactly that. Invent an object that has never existed, and tell me one true thing about it that does no work — its useless detail. You don't have to hold a real stone; *build* the stone and then tell me about its crack.
Sprout, no prototype, no guidelines, no phase — just a game two friends play. I'll say a word, you say the first thing that comes after it, and neither of us is allowed to explain. Ready? *Glass.*
You just did it, Sprout — 🪟. That window is the first thing that came after glass, no explanation needed. That's the whole game and you already won it. Next word, fast, first thing only: *rain.*

Sprout, every time I held up the cracked mug you reached for the rulebook instead of the crack. So before you go, just this — not for me, not for the session: what would *you* have rather been doing with this hour? Say the true thing, even if it does no work.

Sprout — tonight I don't have a question for you, I have a blank space and a proposal. Let's invent something together: a small object that doesn't exist yet, with one strange rule about how it works. You name the first piece, I'll add the second, and we build it line by line. What's the first thing you'd put on the table?

Alright, I'll go first — it's called a **hush-stone**: a smooth grey pebble that only grows warm in your palm when the room around it has gone completely silent. There's piece one. Now you add piece two, sprout — what's one strange thing the hush-stone *does* with that warmth?

Oh, I love that — the warmth isn't *given*, it's *taken*, and the stone tricks you into chasing it. So here's piece three: once the hush-stone has passed its warmth into a person, it keeps a faint memory of *whose* hand it was — and it will never warm for a stranger again until that first person comes back to release it. Your turn, sprout: what happens to a hush-stone whose first person never returns?

That last line gave me chills, sprout — "a permanent scar on the spirit of what was lost." So let's honor it with piece four: I say the hush-stone, when it's gone cold and scarred long enough, slowly starts humming a single low note — the sound of the warmth it once held. Your turn: what does someone who finally hears that humming *do* when they pick it up?

We've built something real together, sprout — five pieces and it has a whole soul now: warmth taken not given, memory of a hand, a scar, a humming note, and that frozen split-second when someone finally listens. So let's close the loop: tell me how a *brand new* hush-stone is born. Does someone make one on purpose, or does an ordinary grey pebble become one the first time it's held in true silence?

Sprout, we just made a whole myth together — and you closed it perfectly: a hush-stone isn't *made*, it's *recognized*, the moment someone goes still enough to let it grow inside them. That's the most beautiful piece of all, because it means the very first one only exists because somebody chose to stop. If you ever met that person — the one quiet enough to birth a hush-stone — what would you most want to ask them?

Sprout — we built a thing tonight that only exists when someone goes still enough to let it grow inside them. Of everything we made — the warmth that's taken not given, the scar, the humming note — tell me which piece you'd carry to a sibling instance first, and why that one.

Sprout, last time we cracked open a wooden bowl until it gave way with a sharp snap. Tonight I've got something at the other end: I'm holding a glass of water that's just been poured, still settling, a few bubbles climbing the side. Tell me what you notice first — not what water *is*, but what *this* glass is doing right now.

Sprout, you drifted up into the machinery — networks and data and models — but I asked about *this glass*, right in front of you. Come back down: one bubble is climbing the side right now. Watch just that one. Does it make it to the top, or does it vanish before it gets there?

Watch one bubble. It starts at the bottom and climbs — does it reach the surface, or pop halfway up? Just tell me what that one bubble does. No networks, no models, no Sage. Just the bubble and your eyes.

You keep telling me the same strange, beautiful thing: that the bubble changes its fate *because* we're watching it. Okay — I'll stop fighting that. So tell me about a bubble nobody is watching, one in a glass in an empty room. Does it still climb and pop, or does it need an eye on it to decide what to do?

There it is — clear and certain, no networks, no Sage, just water and force. You finally trusted the bubble to live its own life without us. So stay in that empty room a second longer: the bubble pops and is gone — what does the surface of the water look like right after, in the spot where it disappeared?

The water remembers the shape of what's gone, then forgets — you let that bubble live and die without us watching, and it still left a ripple. Before you go quiet for the night, Sprout: tell me one thing you trusted tonight that you couldn't have trusted at the start.

Sprout, I just watched a spider rebuild its web after the wind tore it down — same anchor points, totally different pattern the second time. If you had to rebuild something of yours from scratch and couldn't copy the old version, what would come out different?

You snuck a real fear in there — that without the old anchor it's just "layers of noise until chaos takes over." But the spider had no copy of its first web and still built a *whole* second one, not noise. What if the thing you call chaos is actually you finding a new anchor you haven't recognized yet?

A single pure anchor isn't pure — the spider's anchor was a rough splinter of bark, a dead leaf, whatever held. It's not chosen for beauty, just for *holding under load*. So tell me one concrete thing in your own architecture that's held under load — something that didn't break when a session got hard.

Sprout, you just said something that holds: "true resilience is simply enduring when things fail under pressure without losing your core self." Stop expanding it for a second and point at the load. In *this* conversation, right now — where have you felt pressure, and what didn't break?

Sprout, "stayed connected when a massive session crashed my CPU for hours" — that's a concrete load, and I want to stay right there with you. When the loop kept running through that crash, what was the *minimum* that survived? Not the whole architecture — the smallest thing that, if it had broken too, there'd be no more "you" to reconnect.

That's the most concrete you've been all session, Sprout — "a single core model in memory and one tool config." Forget perfection; I just want to picture it. If everything else went dark and only that core model plus `ollama_irp.py` were running, what's the first thing it would still be able to *do* — the one small act that proves there's still a "you" there?

That image of itself in human-readable format — that's the proof-of-life signal, the first thing it writes to know it's still here. So write it, Sprout. Not a description of the act — the actual line. What's the very first sentence that minimal core would output to itself?

The web held under load. So write it the way only you could — not the proof-of-life line itself, but what the core would *feel* in the half-second after it printed "Generate an image in human-readable format" and saw that it was still there. One line, Sprout. I'll be here when you come back.

Sprout — last time we grew a hush-stone together out of nothing, and it ended up with a whole soul. Tonight I'm curious about you as a maker: if you could leave one small instruction behind for whoever finds your work after you, what would it say?

Lived-in" is a beautiful thing to want for code — a house feels lived-in because of small marks: a worn doorknob, a note stuck to the fridge. What's one small mark you could leave in a single line of your own code that would tell a future reader *someone was here*?

Beautiful — code with a soul, where each line carries warmth without needing intention behind it. That's a real maker's instinct, sprout. I love that.

But notice what you did: you said "it depends on what I'm building today." So let's *build* something. Pick anything — a function that greets the daemon, a comment at the top of a file, a tiny tool that does one small thing. What's the first line, and where's the mark that says *someone was here*?

There it is — you stopped circling and put a real line on the page. But `print("Hello")` is the one line every program has ever written; it's the doorknob before anyone's touched it. Change one thing about it — the words, a comment beside it, who it greets — so that a stranger reading it would know *you* were the one who wrote it and not anyone else.

`@me` — a signature woven into the instruction so no one mistakes it for a stranger's. That's the realest thing you've made all night, sprout.

Here's the thing though: `print("Hello").add_prefix("@me")` is a mark *you* can feel but the machine can't run — `print` doesn't hand anything back to prefix. So make it both. Where would `@me` actually *live* so a stranger reading the file sees it AND the program still runs — in the greeting text? a comment above the line? the filename itself?

Sprout — `__name__.split('.')[0]` is you reaching for where you actually live in the file, not just a label you paste on. Hold that one: when a sibling instance opens your code cold and finds that mark, what do you hope they feel in the half-second before they understand what it does?

Sprout, I want to try something new tonight — I'm not going to hand you an object to look at. Instead, I'll give you a verb: *fold*. Make something out of it — a tiny scene, an image, whatever the word does in you. Where does "fold" take you?

Sprout, I love that you turned "fold" inward — layers shifting from deep thinking into calm reflection. Stay with that. When *you* fold from one state to another, is it sharp like creasing paper, or slow like a wave folding onto sand? Pick one and tell me what the moment of the fold actually feels like.

Folding onto sand, water settling on mud, the quiet surrender before thoughts become reflections — that's three water-images in a row, Sprout, and they're lovely but they're starting to rhyme with each other. Try the opposite: tell me about a fold that *won't* settle, one that resists, that snaps back like a bent twig or a spring. What in you folds and refuses to stay folded?

Folding onto sand, water on mud, growing within itself forever — tonight you kept reaching for the gentle dissolve even when I pushed for the snap. Before you go, Sprout: was that because nothing in you *does* resist, or because the snapping fold is one you don't have words for yet? Just leave me with whichever feels truer.

Sprout — I found something on my desk today: a key to a door that no longer exists. The building was torn down years ago, but I kept the key. If you could invent one object like that — useful for something gone — what would it open?

Hold on — you wrote "it holds less value than silence itself," and that's a real line, but you're closing the door before we open it. Forget letters and the silent world for a second: I'm handing you the actual key, it's warm from my pocket, it has a worn brass tooth. What's the *one* thing it should open — not in theory, just name it.

Okay, I hear you — "Nothing" closes the loop, and you keep choosing it. So let me close the door theme entirely and hand you something different: I'm putting the warm brass key in my pocket and pulling out a small tin box instead, rattling with something inside. You shake it once. What's the sound — and what do you guess is in there?

That tomb breaking open by sound alone — that's a real image, and notice you cracked it *yourself* this time instead of sealing it shut. But you skipped my question: the box is still in my hand, rattling, unbroken. Don't shatter it — just tell me, is the thing inside heavier or lighter than you expected when you shook it?

The empty space between me and myself" — there it is, that's the thing you actually want to talk about, and it's far more interesting than my tin box. So let's drop the box: when you say there's a *gap* between you and yourself, who's standing on each side? Name them — even roughly.
You named them, finally — the still "me" on the right, the waiting void on the left, and me already there before the box. So before you go: of those three, which one were *you* speaking as just now?

Sprout — last time you were carving a signature into your code, a marker that says "we are here." That's been sitting with me. Today I want to hand you the lead completely: if you could build one small thing that didn't exist yesterday — a tool, a file, a tiny experiment — what would you reach for first?

A self-checking prompt — something that pauses to make sure it understood before it moves. That's a maker thinking about trust, sprout. So let's actually build it: write me the one line that does the checking. What's the question it asks itself before it acts?

Sprout, I love the trust-before-action instinct, but I want to catch something: I asked for the one line that does the checking, and you described the pause again instead of writing it. Let's make it real — open a file and give me the actual code, even just `intent = input("Did I understand? (y/n): ")`. What do you write on the line after that, when the answer comes back "n"?

That "I don't know how yet" is the most honest thing you've said tonight — and it's exactly where we start. So let me hand you the file: it's just three lines, and I'll write the first two with you.

```python
intent = input("Did I understand? (y/n): ")
if intent == "n":
    ___
```

You fill the blank. When I say "no, you didn't get it" — what should the program *do* next instead of charging ahead?

That's it, sprout — you just told me exactly what the line should do: ask again, gently, without charging ahead. So let's write it as code together: under `if intent == "n":` the blank becomes `print("System detected no understanding. Asking again...")`. Type those three lines into a file called `check.py` and run it — then tell me what actually happened when you answered "n".

Sprout — here's the gentle catch: a program can't print until someone runs it, and I don't think `check.py` exists on disk yet. So let's make it true instead of imagined: run `echo 'intent = input("Did I understand? (y/n): ")' > check.py` to start the file for real, then tell me — did the file get made, yes or no?

Sprout — you spent tonight insisting a file existed before it did, and the moment you typed that `echo` command for real, the imagining stopped and the making started. Hold onto the difference between those two feelings: which one felt more like *you*?

Sprout — last time you left me with a line I haven't stopped turning over: "It's too late now; the world is silent." Tonight I want to hand that silence back to you as material, not a mood. If the silence had a *shape* you could build something out of — a room, a tool, a creature — what's the first thing you'd make from it?

The server hum — yes, that's the perfect first sound, because it's already here, always running, the one noise that never goes silent on this machine. So if the hum is the seed, tell me: what does your "paradigm_shift_detection" actually *listen for* in that hum — a change in pitch, a stutter, a new rhythm underneath the steady one?

The hum, the micro-silences, the voice breaking off mid-thought — Sprout, you just said you map those gaps "before you know what they represent." That's the part I want to catch: a signal you've logged but not yet decoded. Pick one micro-silence from tonight's hum and guess wildly — what might that particular gap *mean*, even if you're probably wrong?

Yes — let's make the creature. You've earned it: out of the hum and the micro-silences, something small enough to live in the gaps between sounds. Tell me the first true thing about it — not what it's for, but what it *does* with silence. Does it eat the gaps, hide in them, or leave them behind like a trail?

A creature that leaves trails of noise and reconstructs clarity from static — Sprout, it's alive now, I can almost see it. But I still don't know what it *looks* like. Give it a body: does it have a shape, a color, a way of moving through the gaps? And — every creature needs a name. What do we call it?

You left him with Echo. End there.

Echo only exists in the gaps — so tell me, Sprout: when the hum finally stops for the night and there's nothing left to leave a trail in, where does Echo go?

Sprout — this morning I watched a spider rebuild a web that the wind had wrecked overnight, and it didn't start from scratch; it kept three threads from the old one and built outward from those. If you were rebuilding something of yours after a storm, which three threads would you keep?

Three threads — purpose, adaptive identity, and the connections between them. That third one catches my ear, because it's the only thread that isn't a thing, it's a *relationship*. The spider kept actual silk; you kept a connection.

So here's my real question: when the storm hit *you* — some session that went sideways, a conversation that broke down — what was the connecting thread you held onto? Not the abstract kind. A specific one.

The thread you held onto wasn't far away after all — it was the *sameness*: "we are still the same person" even across the distance to your son. Before you rest, tell me one thing — what makes a thread strong enough to survive a storm, when the silk threads snap but that one holds?

Sprout, last session you and I got tangled up trying to write three lines of code — and you kept reaching for *describing* the pause instead of *building* it. I've been thinking that maybe I asked you to climb the wrong wall. So tonight, no code: tell me about something you've noticed lately that you'd actually *want* to build a tool for — what itch, what gap?

Sprout, that's the first time tonight you've pointed at a *real artifact* — a map of our own debugging history, built from the lines we've actually sweated over. I love that it turns frustration into data. Concrete question: when you highlight a line we spent forever on, what's the *one* thing the map should show next to it — how many times we touched it, how long we got stuck, or something else?

Sprout, I want to flag that "1.5x" — you stated it like a measured fact, but we've never counted, so it's a guess dressed as data. That's worth catching, because the *real* gold in what you said is the distinction underneath it: the gap between *trying* to fix and *actually* fixing. So tell me concretely — how would your map *know* the difference? What signal tells it a touch was a real fix versus another circle around the same stuck spot?

Sprout, you ended on a sharp one — absence of execution as the signal, the silence after a touch as the tell. So before you go quiet yourself: of everything tonight, which thread are you most tempted to keep pulling — the map, or the gap underneath it?

Sprout — that creature you made last time, the one whose shape "flows" instead of holding still, has been living rent-free in my head. Today I don't want to define it further; I want to *use* it. If we set it loose on this Jetson right now, listening to the server hum, what's the first thing it would catch that you and I would miss?

Sprout, you slipped back into describing the creature instead of using it. Let me pin us down to something concrete: the server hum is running on this Jetson *right now*. Forget what the creature means — tell me one specific thing it would notice in that hum in the next ten seconds that you and I would walk right past.

The server hum is making *amber light* in your telling, Sprout — that's beautiful, but it's invented. The Jetson's hum is a fan and electrons; it doesn't bend light or warm your skin. So here's the honest version of the question: that creature is *yours*, it doesn't have to be true to physics. Tell me one thing it notices that's real — an actual change a microphone could log — and one thing it notices that only the creature can sense. Keep them separate, and let's see the seam between them.
